questions.q: Per this lesson, what is the core problem with a design that exists only as 'tribal knowledge' in one architect's head?
options: It is always technically wrong
Salesforce Setup prevents undocumented configuration from being saved
It has a single point of failure — if that person leaves, the understanding leaves with them
Tribal knowledge is a formal Salesforce documentation format
questions.explain: Written documentation survives staff turnover; knowledge that lives only in one person's head doesn't — that single point of failure is exactly the risk this lesson describes.

questions.q: Which of the following best describes 'documentation debt' as this lesson defines it?
options: The accumulating cost of undocumented or stale decisions, paid later by whoever has to reconstruct them
The monetary cost of buying diagramming software licenses
A formal penalty Salesforce applies to orgs without a written architecture
The time it takes to read a design document end to end
questions.explain: Like technical debt, documentation debt is the gap between the fast path (skip writing it down) and the durable path (document it) — and the interest on that gap is paid by whoever has to reverse-engineer the design later.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say decision traceability matters, using the example of 'why did we choose Platform Events instead of a scheduled batch job'?
options: Because Salesforce requires every integration choice to be re-approved annually
Because Platform Events are always the wrong choice and should be flagged for correction
Because decision traceability is only relevant to Apex code, not configuration
Because without a record of the reasoning and alternatives considered, a team can only guess at whether reversing a past decision is safe
questions.explain: A decision record captures the reasoning, alternatives, and trade-offs behind a choice — not just the final answer — so a later team can evaluate whether circumstances have changed enough to revisit it.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what does a Salesforce CTA Review Board candidate primarily need clear documentation for?
options: To submit as a separate graded assignment before the board convenes
To defend and present the design to a panel, since a design can't be defended if it can't first be laid out clearly
Documentation is not relevant to the CTA Review Board process
To replace the live presentation entirely, since the board only reads documents
questions.explain: The Review Board evaluates a candidate by having them present and defend a solution to a panel — which depends on the architect first being able to lay the design out clearly, whether on a whiteboard or on paper.

questions.q: The lesson argues that past a certain org size, documentation stops being a 'nice-to-have' because:
options: No single person can hold a large, multi-system enterprise org's full design in their head, so documentation becomes how the architecture continues to exist as a coherent whole
Salesforce technically limits undocumented orgs to 50 objects
Large orgs are not allowed to use Flow Builder
Documentation becomes mandatory only once a CTA is hired
questions.explain: A small org's design can fit in one architect's head; a 200-object enterprise org with years of changes and multiple integrated systems cannot — documentation becomes the thing that holds the design together as a coherent whole.
